gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of each kit's price is really the panel, or how long that panel takes to refill its own station, for the Elite 200 V2, Elite 30 V2 and ALLPOWERS P1800 kits. On 2026-11-14 the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit charges $300 for its panel ($1.50/W). That panel needs at least 10.4 hours at full rated output to refill the 2,073.6 Wh station, and it uses only 20% of the station's 1,000 W solar input. The ALLPOWERS P1800 + 400 W kit charges $0.75/W for its panel and refills in 2.6 hours at full rated output.
standout_why: StormWatts (cited, 2026-10-16) covers the same metrics: the panel's cost inside the bundle in $/W, and refill % at 4.5 sun-hours with 85% efficiency. But it only covers EcoFlow, Jackery and the BLUETTI AC180 kits, so for the AC180 + 200 W this angle adds nothing new apart from today's price. GetWattLogic (cited) gives only a general sizing rule: panel W ≥ battery Wh ÷ 3, and '2+ sunny days' for a 100 W panel on 1,000 Wh. Trek4Tech gives rough refill hours ('five-plus hours' for 200 W on about 1,000 Wh) and solar input limits, but no prices. None of the three gives the panel's implied price, refill time or share of solar input for the Elite 200 V2, Elite 30 V2, P1800 or C1000 Gen 2 kits. Our current page has the kit savings but not these derived figures.
decides: This supports 'buy the kit only when its panel fits the station.' The implied panel price in every kit checked ($0.66–$2.00/W) is at or below BLUETTI's own standalone 200 W panel ($399, $2.00/W), so the kit is the cheaper way to get the maker's panel. But the Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit pairs a 2,073.6 Wh battery with a panel that uses only 20% of its solar input and needs more than a full day of rated sun to refill. A buyer who wants to recharge from solar should pick the 2× 200 W ($1,499) or 350 W ($1,449) kit, or add a panel separately. The P1800 + 400 W and + 600 W kits are the best fit: the panel is cheap per watt and covers 62–92% of the solar input.
